From a radical feminist perspective, womanhood is not a feeling, a performance, or a personal identity category; it is a political and material reality rooted in biological sex. It does insist, however, that compassion for one group must not come at the expense of another group’s ability to name, maintain, and defend its own boundaries as a sex class.

1. Why radical feminism grounds womanhood in biological sex

Radical feminism is centrally concerned with male power over female bodies: their labor, sexuality, fertility, and physical vulnerability. The root analysis is simple: males, as a class, have historically dominated females, as a class, through control over reproduction and sexuality and through the threat or reality of male violence. These are not abstract concepts; they are materially rooted in sex:

  • Females are the ones who become pregnant and bear children.
  • Females experience menstruation, menopause, and pregnancy-related risks.
  • Females, on average, have less upper-body strength and different size/strength profiles than males, affecting vulnerability in physical confrontations.
  • Females face sex-specific forms of violation such as rape and pregnancy resulting from rape.

On this view, “woman” names those adult humans who share this material condition: being biologically female. This shared condition is what underlies sex-based oppression and therefore what underlies sex-based rights and protections. If “woman” is redefined to include males, the connection between the category and the material basis of women’s oppression is weakened or erased.

Radical feminists therefore argue:

  • If patriarchy targets females because of their sexed bodies, then combating patriarchy requires recognizing and organizing around that same sexed reality.
  • Recasting womanhood as a subjective identity rather than a material political category shifts the focus away from structural male dominance and towards individual feelings and self-definitions, making collective female organizing more difficult.

2. The political importance of sex-based categories

Laws and policies designed to protect women are typically grounded in the recognition that females, as a class, have specific vulnerabilities and experiences. These include:

  • Rape crisis centers and domestic violence shelters tailored to female survivors of male violence.
  • Female-only hospital wards, changing rooms, and showers.
  • Sex-based data collection on violence, discrimination, pay gaps, and health outcomes.
  • Title IX and similar frameworks enabling female-only sports categories.
  • Prison policies recognizing the risks women face from male inmates.

In each case, the underlying rationale is sex, not identity. The question is not how a person feels, but what their body is, what risks they pose or face, and how male socialization and physical differences manifest in particular contexts.

From a radical feminist viewpoint, redefining “woman” to be a category any male can enter simply by self-identifying undermines the coherence and effectiveness of these protections. If “woman” no longer reliably tracks biological sex, then:

  • Female-only statistics become blurred, affecting our ability to track male violence against women as a distinct phenomenon.
  • Sex-specific services for females become open to males, regardless of women’s comfort and privacy.
  • Policies that were designed to address female vulnerability may end up prioritizing the desires or identities of males who self-identify into the category.

In short, the sex class “women” becomes politically incoherent if anyone of the opposite sex can claim membership on the basis of internal feeling.

3. Transgender women and the question of biological sex

From this radical feminist standpoint, transgender women are understood as biologically male—adult human males—who identify psychologically or socially as women. This has several implications:

  1. Sex is not altered by identity.

Sex is determined by gamete-producing reproductive anatomy (current or developmental), chromosomes, and a range of dimorphic traits that exist regardless of self-perception.

  2. Male socialization still matters.
    Many transgender women have lived a significant portion of their lives being treated as male, often benefiting from male socialization and male privilege in education, work, and public spaces. Radical feminists contend that this history affects behavior, expectations, and unconscious entitlement, in ways that are relevant when we consider women-only spaces that are intended as refuges from male presence.

  3. Physical differences do not vanish.
    Even with medical transition, aspects of male physiology—such as bone structure, muscle mass, height, and reach—often remain. In contexts like sports, prisons, or shelters, these differences can materially affect safety, fairness, and risk.

Recognizing these realities is not, from this perspective, an act of hatred; it is a precondition for meaningful sex-based analysis. The central claim is that biological sex continues to matter socially and politically, and that ignoring sex in favor of identity can expose women to risks and erode their capacity to organize as a distinct class.

4. Female-only spaces: privacy, dignity, and safety

Female-only spaces did not arise from arbitrary prejudice; they emerged from concrete needs connected to women’s vulnerability to male violence and women’s need for privacy from the male gaze. Radical feminists argue that opening these spaces to males who self-identify as women undermines those purposes.

a. Rape crisis centers and domestic violence shelters

These spaces are often designed by and for female survivors of male violence. Many survivors have trauma triggers specifically linked to male bodies, male voices, and male socialization. For them:

  • The presence of a male-bodied person can be experienced as threatening or retraumatizing, regardless of how that person identifies.
  • The ability to say “no males” is part of what allows some survivors to even seek help.

From a radical feminist viewpoint, requiring women to accept male-bodied individuals in these spaces:

  • Prioritizes the identity claims of males over the trauma-informed needs of females.
  • Compromises the very rationale for having female-only services in the first place.

The core argument is not that transgender women are inherently dangerous; rather, it is that women, especially traumatized women, should not be compelled to share intimate, vulnerable spaces with male bodies at all.

These facilities implicate bodily privacy in states of partial or full undress. Radical feminists emphasize:

  • Women and girls have sex-based rights to privacy from male bodies, especially in vulnerable states.
  • Many females, for cultural, religious, or personal reasons, are deeply uncomfortable being undressed in the presence of male-bodied individuals.

If access is based on self-declared identity rather than biological sex, any male can enter female facilities simply by asserting a female identity. This raises several concerns:

  • It becomes difficult, if not impossible, to challenge males who may exploit such policies for voyeuristic or predatory purposes.
  • Women’s comfort and consent around who sees their naked or semi-naked bodies is subordinated to a self-identification claim.

Again, the issue is not to declare transgender women predators as a class, but to recognize that sex-based boundaries are one of the few practical tools women have to protect their privacy and reduce opportunities for male abuse.

Beyond safety and privacy, radical feminists argue that redefining “woman” to center identity rather than sex dilutes women’s political identity.

a. The problem of redefining “woman”

If “woman” is defined as anyone who identifies as a woman, then:

  • The category no longer maps onto female-bodied people as the group subject to sex-based oppression.
  • It becomes impossible to speak clearly about issues like pregnancy, childbirth, female genital mutilation, menstruation, or menopause as women’s issues without being accused of exclusion.

Radical feminists contend that this linguistic and conceptual shift:

  • Obscures the specific sex-based oppression females face.
  • Makes it harder to organize politically around shared female experiences.
  • Reframes women’s rights as a subset of “gender identity” rights, rather than as responses to sex-based oppression by males.

b. The impact on feminist organizing

Many forms of feminist organizing—consciousness-raising groups, women’s conferences, political caucuses—have historically relied on women having the ability to meet as a sex class to analyze their oppression without male presence. When “woman” is redefined to include males:

  • Women-only political spaces may be pressured to admit males who identify as women.
  • Women who say they need female-only spaces can be labeled bigoted and silenced.
  • The focus of feminist activism can shift from challenging male dominance to accommodating the needs and sensitivities of males who identify as women.

From a radical feminist angle, this reverses priorities: instead of addressing the structurally entrenched power of males over females, energy and resources are increasingly directed toward ensuring that males who identify as women are fully validated as women in all contexts.

6. Balancing compassion and boundaries

Radical feminists can recognize that transgender people may suffer real distress and discrimination and still insist on sex-based boundaries and definitions. The core claims are:

  • Respect for transgender people does not require redefining womanhood away from biological sex.
  • Protecting sex-based female spaces is not about hatred; it is about acknowledging women’s vulnerability to male violence and the political necessity of women organizing as a sex class.

  • Clear, sex-based criteria for spaces like shelters, prisons, competitive sports, and intimate facilities, with tailored solutions where possible, rather than blanket identity-based access.

7. Conclusion: why sex still matters

From a radical feminist perspective, the attempt to redefine womanhood purely in terms of gender identity is not a neutral or harmless linguistic adjustment; it reshapes the terrain on which women fight for their rights. Because women’s oppression is rooted in their biological sex, the category “woman” must remain anchored in that material reality if it is to serve as a basis for political analysis and collective action.

Transgender women, on this view, are biologically male individuals who deserve to live without cruelty or unjust discrimination. But recognizing their dignity does not require erasing the sex-based category of women or dissolving female-only spaces. When inclusion demands that females surrender their boundaries, privacy, and ability to name their own political reality, it ceases to be inclusion and becomes a new form of constraint on women.

The radical feminist argument is thus that sex-based womanhood is not negotiable, and that female-only spaces are essential to protecting women’s rights, safety, and identity. In a world where male violence and sex-based inequality remain pervasive, dismantling those boundaries in the name of gender identity risks sacrificing the interests of women as a sex class in favor of a politics that no longer centers their material reality.

Female-only spaces—shelters, locker rooms, prisons, and sports—were established to protect women from male violence and ensure equitable opportunities. The Erosion of Women’s Rights and Identity

If womanhood is reduced to a self-declared identity, the political power of women as a class dissolves.

Radical feminism demands unapologetic advocacy for women as a sex class. This does not negate the humanity of transgender individuals but insists that their inclusion in female spaces cannot come at the expense of women’s rights. Compassion and justice require policies that protect all marginalized groups without sacrificing the needs of one for another. Self-identification removes that boundary entirely and asks women to accept the increased risk on faith.

A. The Deconstruction of "Woman"

The redefinition of "woman" to include biological males has cascading linguistic and conceptual effects. Women are increasingly referred to as "uterus-havers," "menstruators," "birthing bodies," "cervix-owners," and "people who bleed." These dehumanizing circumlocutions are applied exclusively to women; no one refers to men as "prostate-havers" or "ejaculators" in medical or political discourse. Women—and only women—are being linguistically dismembered to accommodate the identities of biological males.

This is not inclusive language; it is the erasure of a political class. If women cannot name themselves, they cannot organize. If "woman" means nothing more than a feeling anyone can claim, then the category loses its analytical and political utility. As the writer and feminist Victoria Smith has argued, "You cannot fight for the rights of a group you are not allowed to define."

Women who articulate these positions—including academics, writers, athletes, politicians, healthcare professionals, and ordinary citizens—face extraordinary professional and social consequences. Kathleen Stock, a philosophy professor at the University of Sussex, was driven from her position for arguing that biological sex is real and politically relevant. Maya Forstater lost her job for stating that sex is immutable, a position later vindicated by a UK employment tribunal. J.K. Rowling has faced years of sustained harassment, including death and rape threats, for defending sex-based rights. Women across professions have been fired, deplatformed, investigated, and ostracized for articulating positions that were, until very recently, uncontroversial feminist orthodoxy.

The pattern is unmistakable: women who attempt to maintain the boundaries of their own political category are punished. This is not progressive; it is a new iteration of a very old dynamic—women being silenced for refusing to center male needs and demands.

A. "Trans Women Are Women"

This slogan functions as a tautology that forecloses analysis. It presupposes the conclusion it seeks to establish. Whether transgender women are women is precisely the question at issue, and it cannot be resolved by assertion. If "woman" is a biological category, then biological males are not women regardless of identity. If "woman" is an identity category, then feminism loses its subject. The radical feminist position is that the former definition is both more coherent and more politically useful.

B. "Excluding Trans Women Is Bigotry"

Recognizing the material reality of biological sex is not bigotry; it is the foundation of women's rights. Sex-based protections exist because of biological reality, not identity. Acknowledging that a biological male is male is a factual observation, not an act of hatred. It is possible to support the civil rights and dignified treatment of transgender people while maintaining that biological sex has legal, medical, and political significance. These positions are not contradictory.

C. "Trans Women Face Violence Too"

This is true, and it is a serious concern. But the violence transgender women face is overwhelmingly perpetrated by men—the same class from which women's spaces are designed to provide refuge. The solution to male violence against transgender women is not to compromise the safety of biological women; it is to address male violence directly and, where necessary, to create appropriate third-space accommodations.

The existence of intersex conditions (DSDs) does not invalidate the sex binary any more than the existence of rare developmental anomalies invalidates any other biological category. The vast majority of humans are unambiguously male or female, and sex is determined by reproductive role, not by edge cases. Moreover, the vast majority of transgender individuals are not intersex; they are biologically typical males or females who identify differently from their sex. The invocation of intersex conditions as an argument for gender self-identification is both scientifically misleading and instrumentalizing of people with genuine medical conditions.

A feminism worthy of the name must be capable of identifying its subject. Women are not a feeling, a costume, or a performance. Women are the sex class that is oppressed on the basis of their reproductive biology—that is impregnated, menstruates, gestates, gives birth, and lactates; that is subjected to sexual violence, reproductive coercion, and systemic subordination because of these biological realities. The radical feminist position on sex and gender is neither novel nor extreme. It is the position that animated a century of feminist activism: that women are a sex class, that our oppression is rooted in biology, and that our liberation requires the ability to name and organize around that reality. The contemporary movement to redefine womanhood on the basis of subjective identity—and to open female-only spaces to any male who claims a female identity—represents not progress but the dissolution of the very category upon which women's rights depend.

Women did not fight for generations to see the word "woman" rendered meaningless, their spaces opened to male bodies by bureaucratic fiat, and their voices silenced when they object. A feminism that cannot define its subject cannot defend its subject. The defense of sex-based rights is not a relic of the past; it is the urgent, necessary, and principled work of the present.
